MOBILE TIRE VAN JOB PICKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

One van, ten requests: which jobs should it run today?

Taking calls in the order they ring, or the biggest ticket first, fills the day with the wrong work. Paste the queue — price, materials, minutes on site, the window each customer gives you and where they are — and get the exact set and order of jobs with the highest profit for the day, the drive and idle time it implies, what each job it turns down would need to pay, and what first-come dispatch leaves behind.

For mobile tire, roadside service and other one-van field businesses. Nothing is uploaded: the text box is analysed in this browser and never leaves your device.

    Prefer a CLI?

    Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

    node cli.mjs plan jobs.csv --start 08:00 --end 17:00 --hourly 35 --per-mile 0.70 --json
cat jobs.csv | node cli.mjs plan - --speed 25

    Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. More: Which mobile tire jobs should a van take? Window and drive-time math.

    What's recognised

    InputHandling

    The plan is exact for the numbers you type (a search over every set and order, up to 14 jobs). One van and one depot; real traffic, one-way streets, a second technician, jobs that must follow each other, customer cancellations and the value of a repeat customer are not modelled. Distance is straight-line miles times your circuity factor, not a routing service.

    Common questions

    Does it upload my job list?

    No. The browser page works on the text you paste, in your own browser, and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

    How is the best day found?

    The tool tries the jobs as a search over which have been done and which was last, keeping every way to get there that is not both later and less profitable than another. That finds the exact best set and order for the numbers you give, and the tests compare it with trying every ordering of every subset.

    Why would it turn down a job I would normally take?

    Because a van can only be in one place. A job that pays well but drives you across the map, or sits in a window that collides with two better jobs, can cost more than the two it displaces. The tool says what the job would need to pay to earn its place.

    Where do the costs come from?

    From your own books: fuel and wear per mile, and the hourly cost of the van and the technician. They are your estimates, so treat the plan as a decision aid, not a forecast.

    Who is it for?

    Mobile tire and roadside service operators, mobile mechanics and other one-van field-service businesses choosing which requested jobs to run today.

which-mobile-tire-jobs-should-a-van-take.text:
Mobile Tire Van Job Picker · guide

Which mobile tire jobs should a van take? Window and drive-time math

Short answer: pick the set and order of jobs whose combined margin, after the drive between them, is highest and that all fit their windows and get the van home on time. A van does one thing at a time, so a good job can be a bad choice if it displaces two better ones.

A worked queue

Ten requests, one van leaving at 08:00 and due back at 17:00, costing $35 an hour while driving or working and $0.70 a mile, driving 30 mph over roads 1.3 times the straight-line distance. Prices range from a $55 valve stem to a $620 four-tire truck job.

  • Taking calls in the order they came in fits 6 jobs and earns $308.45.
  • Biggest tickets first fits 3 jobs and earns $127.33: it takes the $620 truck job first, a long drive out with a 10:00 window, and that leaves room for only two more.
  • The best day runs 8 jobs, starting with the rush roadside spare swap, and earns $486.23 over 86.2 miles, home at 16:57. That is $177.77 more than the best simple rule.

The four-tire truck job is turned down in the best day, and would earn a place only at about $652.65, so the quote to give is that, not the $620 asked. The $55 valve stem 15 miles out loses money even as the only job and would need about $97.66.

What to feed it

  1. Hourly cost: van payment, insurance, technician wages and benefits divided by hours actually worked, not hours paid.
  2. Per-mile cost: fuel plus tires and maintenance per mile driven.
  3. For each job, the window from the customer and the miles east and north from your depot.

Check any motor-club or fleet agreement first: some require you to answer certain calls, and a stranded or unsafe driver comes before any optimum.

Questions

How do I decide which mobile tire calls to take?

Compare whole days, not single calls: for a set of jobs in a given order, add what each pays after materials and on-site time, subtract the drive between them, and check every time window. The best day is the best such set and order. The picker finds it exactly for up to 14 jobs.

Is taking the biggest tickets first a good rule?

Not reliably. Big tickets often sit far from each other or in the same window, so the van drives and waits for them. On the worked queue it earns $127.33 against $486.23 for the best day.

What should a job pay to be worth a detour?

The picker prints, for each job it turns down, the price at which the best day would include it. That is the number to quote for a far or awkward call, or the number to give a fleet that asks for a discount.

The worked example is illustrative arithmetic, not a forecast.
